relearning.title: Read: prokaryotic vs. eukaryotic cells
relearning.description: A short reading with the studio-apartment analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

sections.title: One open room vs. a house with rooms

body.text:
**I can compare and contrast prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.**

**Think of a studio apartment and a house.** A studio is one open room: the bed, the kitchen and everything else share the same space. A house has separate rooms with doors. A **prokaryotic** cell is the studio: its DNA sits out in the open, and there are no inner rooms. A **eukaryotic** cell is the house: its DNA has its own room (the **nucleus**), and jobs happen in separate rooms called **membrane-bound organelles**.

**Prokaryotic cells.** No nucleus. The DNA (one circular loop) sits in a region of the cytoplasm called the **nucleoid**. No membrane-bound organelles. Small, about 1 to 10 micrometers. Examples: **bacteria** and archaea. Many have a cell wall, and some have a **flagellum** to swim.

**Eukaryotic cells.** A nucleus surrounded by a nuclear membrane. Membrane-bound organelles like mitochondria, ER and the Golgi apparatus. Larger, about 10 to 100 micrometers. Examples: **plants, animals, fungi and protists**.

**What ALL cells share:** a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.

**Word trick.** Pro- means before and karyon means nucleus, so prokaryote means before nucleus. Eu- means true, so eukaryote means true nucleus.

**Worked example:** A yeast cell is only one cell, but it has a nucleus and mitochondria. So it is **eukaryotic** (yeast is a fungus). Being single-celled does not make something a prokaryote.

checks.prompt: A cell has a nucleus but no cell wall. What kind of cell is it?

options.text: You can't tell without a cell wall

checks.explanation: A nucleus means eukaryotic. The cell wall doesn't decide it: bacteria, plants and fungi all have cell walls, and animal cells don't. Using the cell wall as the clue is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Which of these do prokaryotic cells NOT have?
checks.explanation: Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles, which prokaryotes don't have. Every cell has ribosomes and a cell membrane. Thinking prokaryotes lack ribosomes is the common mistake: ribosomes have no membrane around them.

sections.title: Comparing them side by side

body.text:
**Alike.** Both are cells. Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA. Both carry out every life process.

**Different.**
**Nucleus:** prokaryotes have none (DNA in the nucleoid). Eukaryotes have one.
**Organelles:** prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotes have many.
**Size:** eukaryotic cells are usually about 10 times bigger.
**DNA:** prokaryotes have one circular loop. Eukaryotes have several long, straight chromosomes inside the nucleus.
**Who:** prokaryotes are bacteria and archaea. Eukaryotes are plants, animals, fungi and protists.

**Why eukaryotes can be more complex.** Separate rooms let a eukaryotic cell do many jobs at once without them getting in each other's way, like a house with a kitchen, a bedroom and a garage.

**Worked example 2: classify an unknown cell.** A cell is 2 micrometers long. It has a cell wall, a flagellum, ribosomes and a loop of DNA, but no nucleus. Ignore the cell wall and the flagellum, since some eukaryotes have them too. The key question is: is there a nucleus? No. So it is a **prokaryote**, most likely a bacterium.

**Worked example 3:** Strep throat is caused by Streptococcus, a bacterium, so its cells are prokaryotic. The cells in your throat are eukaryotic.

**Watch out for:** thinking prokaryotes have no DNA (they have DNA, just no nucleus), thinking prokaryotes have no ribosomes, thinking single-celled always means prokaryote (yeast and amoebas are single-celled eukaryotes), using the cell wall to decide, and calling viruses prokaryotes (viruses aren't cells at all).

checks.prompt: Which features would you find in a Streptococcus bacterium?

options.text: Ribosomes and DNA, but no nucleus

checks.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes: they have ribosomes and DNA like every cell, but no nucleus or other membrane-bound organelles. Thinking bacteria have no DNA is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A cell is about 50 micrometers across and has a nucleus. Which organism could it come from?
checks.explanation: A large cell with a nucleus is eukaryotic, like a plant cell from an oak tree. E. coli is a small prokaryote with no nucleus, and a virus is not a cell at all.

sections.shortAnswer: Name two ways prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells are alike and two ways they are different.

relearning.title: Do: flip the differences, then classify unknown cells
relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then a worked problem one step at a time.

cards.back: A cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Pro- means before: before nucleus. Bacteria and archaea.
A cell with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Eu- means true: true nucleus. Plants, animals, fungi, protists.
The region of a prokaryote's cytoplasm where its circular DNA sits. It has no membrane, so it is not a nucleus.
Cell parts wrapped in their own membrane, like the nucleus, mitochondria, ER and Golgi. Only eukaryotes have them.
A cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.
Prokaryotes: about 1 to 10 micrometers. Eukaryotes: about 10 to 100 micrometers, often about 10 times bigger.
A long, whip-like tail some cells use to move. Many bacteria have one.

checks.prompt: Which structure tells you for sure that a cell is eukaryotic?
checks.explanation: Only eukaryotes have a nucleus. All cells have ribosomes, and both bacteria and plant cells have cell walls, so those don't decide it.
Bacteria are prokaryotes. Yeast and mushrooms are fungi, and amoebas are protists, so they are eukaryotes. Thinking every single-celled organism is a prokaryote is the common mistake.
Every cell needs ribosomes to make proteins. Ribosomes have no membrane around them, so prokaryotes have them too. Thinking prokaryotes have no organelles of any kind is the common mistake.

sections.title: Worked problem: classify the unknown cells

body.problem: Three unknown cells are viewed under a microscope. Cell X: 3 micrometers, a cell wall, ribosomes and DNA loose in the cytoplasm. Cell Y: 40 micrometers, a nucleus, mitochondria, a cell wall and chloroplasts. Cell Z: 20 micrometers, a single-celled organism with a nucleus and mitochondria and no cell wall. Classify each one.

steps.text: Ask the key question first: is there a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles? Ignore the cell wall, because both kinds of cells can have one.
Cell X: no nucleus, DNA loose in the cytoplasm (the nucleoid) and small. It is a prokaryote, most likely a bacterium.
Cell Y: a nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts and a cell wall. It is a eukaryote, a plant cell.
Cell Z: only one cell, but it has a nucleus and mitochondria. It is a eukaryote, likely a protist. Being single-celled doesn't make it a prokaryote.

checks.prompt: Your turn: cell W has a cell wall, a flagellum and ribosomes, but no nucleus. What is it?
checks.explanation: No nucleus means prokaryote. The cell wall and flagellum don't decide it, but ribosomes show it is still a cell. Letting the cell wall decide is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Why is a cell wall NOT a good clue for telling prokaryotes and eukaryotes apart?

options.text: Both bacteria and plant cells have cell walls

checks.explanation: Bacteria (prokaryotes) and plants and fungi (eukaryotes) all have cell walls, so a wall can show up in either kind. The nucleus is the clue that decides.

relearning.title: U3.LT2 Watch: prokaryotic vs. eukaryotic cells

checks.prompt: Where is the DNA in a prokaryotic cell?

options.text: Nowhere, because prokaryotic cells have no DNA
In a region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid

checks.explanation: A prokaryote's DNA is one circular loop that sits in the nucleoid, a region of the cytoplasm with no membrane around it. Thinking prokaryotes have no DNA is the common mistake: they have DNA, just no nucleus.

checks.prompt: A yeast cell is a single cell with a nucleus and mitochondria. What kind of cell is it?

options.text: Prokaryotic, because it is only one cell
Eukaryotic, because it has a nucleus
Neither, because yeast is a fungus

checks.explanation: A nucleus means eukaryotic, and fungi like yeast are eukaryotes. Thinking single-celled always means prokaryote is the common mistake.

sections.title: Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic: The Differences (FuseSchool)

checks.prompt: Which four things do ALL cells have, prokaryotic and eukaryotic?

options.text: A cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA
A nucleus, mitochondria, ER and a Golgi apparatus
A cell wall, a flagellum, ribosomes and DNA

checks.explanation: Every cell has a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA. A nucleus and mitochondria are only in eukaryotes, and not every cell has a cell wall or a flagellum.

checks.prompt: How does the size of a typical eukaryotic cell compare with a prokaryotic cell?

options.text: They are about the same size
The eukaryotic cell is about 10 times bigger
The eukaryotic cell is about 10 times smaller

checks.explanation: Prokaryotes are about 1 to 10 micrometers, and eukaryotic cells are about 10 to 100 micrometers, usually about 10 times bigger.
